https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/j.text: People try to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Thursday. Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AP View image in fullscreen People try to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Thursday. Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AP Spain At least 57 people die as tens of thousands cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco Pedro Sánchez decries ‘violation of territorial integrity’ as other EU countries criticise Madrid over incident Sam Jones in Madrid, Angela Giuffrida in Rome and Jakub Krupa Fri 31 Jul 2026 13.52 EDT First published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 03.59 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least 57 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 50,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco in what Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez , called “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”. The huge influx, which took place over the course of just 24 hours, overwhelmed the city of 85,000 people, triggered a political crisis for Madrid and led to a mixed reaction from other EU countries, including calls for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. 3:37 Tens of thousands of migrants cross into Spanish enclave Ceuta from Morocco - video Sánchez, who arrived in Ceuta on Friday morning, said he would use all the resources at his disposal to guarantee the safety of the city’s population. He attributed the mass crossing to “human trafficking mafias” that had taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta, or Spain’s other north African enclave of Melilla, could not be summarily returned under special rules. Sánchez said: “That has spread like wildfire during these last few hours through the networks of mafias that traffic in human beings and has produced an avalanche of the characteristics and dimension that we experienced yesterday.” Sánchez said a temporary reception centre would be established to facilitate the documentation, registration, triage and “expedited” expulsion of people with no legal claim to be in Spain. Hundreds of migrants run and cheer as they enter Spain’s enclave of Ceuta He also said the government would erect a visible barrier – a line of buoys – near the breakwater at Ceuta’s Tarajal beach to make it clear where the border was, and to legally comply with the court’s ruling. Although the Spanish government said about 50,000 people had crossed the border on Thursday and in the early hours of Friday, the president of Ceuta put the figure at about 60,000. Spain’s interior ministry, which has deployed additional police officers and soldiers to the enclave, said more than 48,300 people had voluntarily returned to Morocco by 6pm on Friday. The Irish presidency of the EU has convened a meeting of member states on Saturday, under the Integrated Political Crisis Response mechanism. EU sources said this will provide experts from member states with an opportunity “to discuss the movements into Ceuta over the last two days, the numbers of people who have returned to Morocco today, the supports being provided by the EU to Spain and diplomatic engagement with Morocco”. A further meeting of EU ambassadors has been called in Brussels on Monday. The latest incident dwarfs the last mass border crossing in May 2021, when Morocco loosened its border controls, allowing about 10,000 people to enter the territory over the course of two days. Map showing location of Ceuta between Spain and Morocco, and another map showing location of Tarajal breakwater in Ceuta That crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed over the territory to Morocco and Mauritania. That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara – a move that had caused a diplomatic rift between Spain and Algeria, which had supported the Polisario group. Sánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first such visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria. Moroccan government sources told the Europa Press news agency that the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations” and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”. Morocco’s ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich, was quoted by the Associated Press as saying that “we have always prioritized legal, orderly and safe migration for all” and indicated that the situation had developed against Rabat’s wishes. View image in fullscreen Spain’s interior ministry said more than 48,300 people decided to return to Morocco from the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Friday. Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AP Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers’ association representing officers of the Spanish Guardia Civil – which patrols Spain’s borders – described the situation as a “serious humanitarian crisis”. Without shelter, thousands of people, including unaccompanied children, had been left sleeping in parks and on pavements, while others roamed the streets aimlessly. “It’s chaotic,” said Sbihi. Among those who died, many drowned, but some were killed in a crush to cross the breakwater fence at Tarajal beach, Sbihi said. View image in fullscreen People waiting on the Moroccan side of the border for a chance to cross to Ceuta. Photograph: Reuters Video footage on Thursday showed crowds of people walking around the breakwaters at Tarajal beach on to local roads. While most appeared to be young men, there were also families with women and small children. Ceuta and Melilla have the E​U’s only land border with ​Africa. ‌Both cities ​periodically ​experience surges in attempted crossings by people seeking to reach Europe . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Crowds in downtown Ceuta on Friday after making the crossing. Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/Reuters The events in Ceuta led some EU countries to issue strong threats or rebukes. Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, summoned Italy’s ambassador to Madrid on Friday after Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now closed scheme to regularise the status of more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”. Tajani’s remarks prompted a sharp response from Albares, who said the comments were “unbecoming” and accused Italy of “partisan demagoguery”. Italy announced on Friday evening that it would be suspending its Schengen arrangements with Spain, but the practical impact of the move was not immediately clear. Meloni said the measure would be kept in force only as long as needed, adding: “In parallel, Italy is ready to support every European initiative to assist Spanish institutions as needed to restore full control of the union’s external borders and to address the ongoing situation with determination.” View image in fullscreen Spanish soldiers patrolling the Spanish-Moroccan border in Ceuta on Friday. Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/Reuters Responding to Italy’s unilateral decision, a European Commission spokesperson said a member state “may exceptionally and temporarily reintroduce internal border control as a matter of last resort, to address serious threats to public order or national security”. But they added that the member state would need to notify the commission and explain how the situation in Ceuta constituted such a threat. The Guardian understands that Italy has not yet formally notified any of its EU partners of its decision. The Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, urged Spain to “act swiftly to regain control of the situation and fulfil its commitments within Schengen cooperation”. The Finnish interior minister, Mari Rantanen, said that as Spain had “completely failed to protect the Schengen area’s external border”, all EU countries should support Italy’s proposal to suspend its Schengen status. However, in a statement later on Friday, the European Commission said Ceuta and Melilla were subject to special Schengen rules that prevented onward movement within the zone. View image in fullscreen Belongings float in the sea after they were left behind by people crossing from Morocco into Ceuta. Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AP The EU’s migration commissioner, Magnus Brunner, called the situation in Ceuta “unacceptable” and said he was in close contact with the Spanish authorities. But he also confirmed there was no onward route from Ceuta given the enclave’s unique status under the Schengen rules. He said: “The Schengen borders code provides for special rules that apply to Ceuta and Melilla. Border checks on persons departing from Ceuta and Melilla remain in force.” But there were also shows of unity. The European Council president, António Costa, expressed his “solidarity with Spain in the current situation of illegal migration in Ceuta”. The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said he had been in touch with the Spanish government to express his solidarity and to offer assistance to Spain. But, as a precautionary measure, Macron said he had asked the interior ministry to strengthen the French controls on its border with Spain with four mobile units and drones. In Spain, the opposition People’s party (PP) called on Sánchez to come up with a tough response, saying the military and police reinforcements announced on Thursday night were insufficient. In a post on X, the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, wrote: “People have continued to arrive in Ceuta throughout the night, and those on the ground describe an occupied city, with nothing sufficient being done to prevent it.” The far-right Vox party called the incident “an invasion”. On Friday evening, hundreds attended an anti-migrant rally outside the Moroccan embassy in Madrid, with images showing some protesters performing Nazi salutes and waving flags with far-right insignia. https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text: An Ebola treatment centre in Rwampara, Ituri, DRC, 20 June 2026. There have been 3,360 confirmed cases of the virus in the east of the country. Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/EPA View image in fullscreen An Ebola treatment centre in Rwampara, Ituri, DRC, 20 June 2026. There have been 3,360 confirmed cases of the virus in the east of the country. Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/EPA Global development Ebola outbreak in DRC the fastest growing in the history of the virus As the death toll rises to almost 1,500, and with a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain potentially still months away, health workers face a battle to slow the outbreak Supported by About this content Prosper Heri Ngorora in Bunia Fri 31 Jul 2026 04.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 04.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The latest numbers of confirmed cases of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has made this latest outbreak the fastest growing in the known history of the virus. At 3,360 confirmed cases , the disease is now affecting people in five provinces in the east of the DRC, with 1,487 deaths recorded, representing an overall case fatality rate estimated at about 45%, according to Congolese health officials. Health responses to the outbreak have been badly hampered by conflict in many of the affected areas. “I fear that at some point, life may come to a standstill here in our province of Ituri,” said Deborah Nzuva, a mother of four who lives in Rwampara, one of the affected regions. “We were already in a precarious situation before the Ebola virus disease, which continues to claim its victims.” Since officially declared by the Congolese authorities on 15 May, the Bundibugyo strain of the virus has spread faster than any of the country’s 16 previous Ebola outbreaks – and the numbers are approaching the previous worst toll, in 2018-2020 when 3,470 people in DRC were infected. Prof Pierre Akilimali, from the country’s public health institute (NPHI), is in charge of the Ebola response. He emphasises that the disease continues to spread and that it is still difficult to know when it will reach its peak. According to him, there is a way to go and the road to bringing the outbreak under control is a long one. View image in fullscreen Members of a Congolese Red Cross team in Bunia carry the body of a woman suspected of having died from Ebola, 7 June. Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty Images “Here in Ituri, we have the issues of insecurity, mining and high population density, which make the current outbreak more complex than previous ones,” he said. The Congolese authorities say they have taken a number of measures to limit spread, including strengthening surveillance through community liaison officers, building more than 20 Ebola treatment centres, and setting up local laboratories for testing. “The public must also play their part by seeking medical advice at the slightest suspicion of infection,” Akilimali said. “This will help us to respond effectively to the disease.” He said cases continue to rise in the Bunia and Rwampara health zones, with between 100 and 150 new confirmed infections each week. Annabelle Nissi, a clothing trader in Bunia, said people were living in fear. “This outbreak is causing us great distress. Our hope lies solely in God’s hands. It continues to disrupt our lives and has brought our development projects to a standstill,” she said. Dr Justus Nsio, field incident manager for the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said it was a race against time. First patients enrolled in record-breaking Ebola treatment trial in DRC Read more “All the experts monitoring this outbreak agree that it was detected too late. When detection is delayed, we have to work hard to make up for what we missed earlier in order to contain the disease,” he said. “What is certain is that, with the commitment of the movement and our partners, the outcome will be favourable.” View image in fullscreen Health workers prepare for a safe burial operation in the community of Mongbwalu, Ituri, DRC, in May. Photograph: Michel Lunanga/Getty Images Clinical trials began in early July of a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no standard treatment. As of 15 July, about 20 people had been enrolled in these trials, which could last up to four months, according to Prof Placide Mbala, head of laboratory operations for the Ebola response in the DRC. Uganda, which this week declared the Ebola outbreak over on its territory, 12 days after its last case was reported, has sent experts to the DRC to work alongside their Congolese counterparts, particularly in the border regions of Tchomia and Kasenyi. Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A hazy Toronto skyline caused by forest fires in northern Ontario, Canada, on 15 July 2026. Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty Images Wildfires Past fires suggest effects of Europe and North America wildfires may linger for years Three years after Maui wildfires many still struggle with ‘biological, emotional and social consequences’, study says Oliver Milman Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 00.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A spate of ferocious wildfires across North America and Europe , worsened by the climate crisis, has incinerated homes and forests and forced thousands of people to flee. Previous fires suggest the effects of these blazes may linger for years to come. The current fires and their plumes of smoke can appear to be a temporary, if immediate, crisis. Nearly 1,000 fires have sprung into life in the boreal forests of Canada, causing the evacuation of towns and toxic smoke to waft into major Canadian and US cities, prompting threats of retribution from Donald Trump, who bizarrely accused Canada of “poisoning” his country’s air. Smoke is billowing from wildfires in the US too, amid the third major heatwave of the past month which has furthered dried out parched vegetation. Vast, lightning-sparked fires across Washington, eastern Oregon and Idaho have caused a plume of smoke so large that it could reach Florida. In Europe, meanwhile, huge fires have gripped parts of the UK , France and Spain , causing the evacuation of more than 250,000 people. View image in fullscreen A house damaged by wildfires in Blagon, south-western France, on Monday. Photograph: Laurent Perpigna/EPA The climate crisis, caused by the burning of fossil fuels, is known to be creating more fire-prone conditions around the world by drying out soils and plants. “The entire Iberian peninsula is suffering the effects of the climate emergency in a very specific way,” said Pedro Sánchez, Spain’s prime minister. Scientists have also long been aware of the unhealthy consequences of wildfire smoke, which can trigger severe respiratory and cardiac problems in affected people. A recent study found that exposure to tiny particles carried in wildfire smoke will raise the risk of hospitalization for older people hundreds of miles away from fires. “The cardiovascular toll of wildfire smoke reaches well beyond the fire lines and well beyond the day the sky turns orange,” said Kai Chen, associate professor of epidemiology at the Yale School of Public Health and study co-author. But identifying the ongoing effects of wildfires long after they have been extinguished has been a more recent understanding. There are continuing challenges in Maui, the second largest of Hawaii’s islands, three years after wildfires there caused more than 100 deaths and razed several thousand buildings, a new report highlights. While living and economic conditions have generally improved since the fires, many people in Maui are still struggling with health concerns such as poorer lung functions, higher blood pressure and mental health challenges, according to the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study , led by researchers at the University of Hawaii and released on Monday. View image in fullscreen An aerial view of vegetation regrowth amid areas destroyed or damaged by the Lahaina wildfire, including the iconic banyan tree, on 4 August 2024 in Lahaina, Hawaii. Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty Images “The progress is real, and it should be recognized,” said Alika Maunakea, co-director of the study and a school of medicine professor at the University of Hawaii. “But the biological, emotional and social consequences of a disaster do not disappear on the same timeline as debris removal or reconstruction.” Nearly half of all adults in the Maui study continued to report depressive symptoms, with nearly one in five experiencing post-traumatic stress. The study, which conducted screenings of more than 2,500 participants, also found severe depressive symptoms and post-traumatic stress increased among children and adolescents, as did blood pressure readings and obesity levels. “Children may appear resilient while still carrying significant emotional and physical effects beneath the surface,” said Christopher Knightsbridge, a mental health therapist based in Lahaina, a coastal town that was largely destroyed by the fires. “Supporting children means supporting the entire family, including their housing, food security, daily routines and access to trusted care,” he added. The researchers stressed that long-term monitoring and intervention is required following a major wildfire event due to impacts that can last for years afterwards. While the skies over North America and Europe will eventually clear of smoke after a tinderbox summer of fire, this climate change-driven era of wildfire is set to exact a lengthy toll. As well as better support for those directly affected by fires, experts say that authorities in smoke-affected areas could respond to the threat of repeated smoke exposure by creating “clean air centers” that people can flee to in order to escape smoke and other air pollutants. A research paper from last year , which found a 7% increase in mortality among a cohort of older people living in southern California over a three-year period due to wildfire smoke exposure, recommended that “activation of public health measures such as clean air centers should not only depend on intensity of smoke, as the long-term effects can be harmful, even at low levels.” Lara Schwarz, an environmental health scientist at UC Berkley who led the research, said: “As wildfires become more frequent and severe in the context of climate change, with California being at high risk, understanding how these harmful wildfires will affect us in the long term is critical to informing better public health action and response.” Explore more on these topics Wildfires France Canada Americas Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Daughter of British couple killed in Spanish wildfire rejects claim they ignored order to leave Europe burns: a visual guide to the wildfires ‘Extremely scary findings’ show climate crisis is supercharging Europe’s wildfire weather ‘We can’t make it better again’: what Europe’s wildfires tell us about the climate crisis Wildfire near Sizewell nuclear plant causes ‘total devastation’ to Suffolk landscape Race to extinguish blazes across Europe as fire weather breaks records Will brutal wildfires force French leaders to take climate crisis seriously? Víctor Jara was arrested and killed by soldiers in the coup that brought the rightwing dictator Augusto Pinochet to power in Chile in 1973. Photograph: Fundacion Victor Jara, Antonio L/AP View image in fullscreen Víctor Jara was arrested and killed by soldiers in the coup that brought the rightwing dictator Augusto Pinochet to power in Chile in 1973. Photograph: Fundacion Victor Jara, Antonio L/AP Chile Pinochet-era soldier jailed for killing folk singer Víctor Jara 53 years ago Nelson Haase Mazzei was sentenced for murdering Jara in 2023, but fled from authorities in Chile John Bartlett in Santiago Mon 27 Jul 2026 12.27 EDT Last modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 05.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 50 years after the murder of the Chilean folk singer Víctor Jara , the last man wanted in connection with his death has been tracked down and brought to justice. Nelson Haase Mazzei, a retired colonel, fled from authorities in 2023 after he and six other retired soldiers were sentenced in absentia for murdering Jara and another man. Chilean police announced on Saturday that Haase Mazzei had been arrested in Puyehue, in the rural south of the country, with a judge ordering his immediate imprisonment. The Víctor Jara Foundation, set up by his widow, the British dancer and activist Joan Jara, said in statement: “We learned that retired Colonel Nelson Haase Mazzei, who had been a fugitive from justice since 2023, was found and imprisoned. We welcome this news. “However, it is important for us to emphasize that, half a century after the murders of Víctor Jara and Littré Quiroga, it is difficult to see this as this justice.” Jara, a singer and leftwing activist, was detained in Santiago, the capital of Chile, on 12 September 1973, the day after Gen Augusto Pinochet’s bloody US-backed coup to depose the socialist president, Salvador Allende. View image in fullscreen Víctor Jara’s widow, Joan, who died in 2023, was a British dancer and activist who set up a foundation in her late husband’s name. Photograph: Roberto Candia/AP Jara was held along with thousands of others at a small covered stadium in central Santiago. Four days later, he was murdered in the changing rooms alongside Allende’s national director of prisons, Littré Quiroga. Haase Mazzei’s arrest is likely to be the final act in the long quest for justice on behalf of Jara, one of the most recognisable victims of the Pinochet dictatorship, which killed or disappeared more than 3,000 people and detained and tortured tens of thousands during 17 years of repressive rule. At the stadium, Jara was tortured and humiliated by officers who played Russian roulette with him before breaking his hands, shattering his skull, and riddling him with automatic gunfire. His body was found dumped near the main cemetery in Santiago with 44 bullet wounds and 56 broken bones. He was 40 years old. The body of Quiroga, who had been shot 23 times, was found at the same time. After evading justice for nearly half a century, seven retired soldiers were found guilty of the murder and sentenced in absentia to varying jail terms in August 2023. Haase Mazzei received a 25-year sentence. He claimed for years that he was not at the stadium, since renamed Estadio Víctor Jara, but sworn testimony placed him at the scene. Haase Mazzei joined the Chilean army’s notorious Tejas Verde brigade in 1972, and was later part of Pinochet’s secret police, the Dirección Nacional de Inteligencia (Dina), where he worked closely with its leader, Manuel Contreras, a renowned regime loyalist who was sentenced to more than 500 years’ jail time for crimes against humanity before his death in 2015. View image in fullscreen Pedro Barrientos being deported from the US to Chile in 2023. Photograph: Policia de Investigaciones de Chile/Reuters Sentenced alongside Haase Mazzei was 86-year-old Hernán Chacón. When police arrived to arrest him at his home in a wealthy district of Santiago in 2023, he asked officers for a moment to take his medication, before slipping off into a side room and taking his own life. Another Tejas Verde officer sentenced for the killing was Pedro Barrientos, who left Chile for the US in 1989 and was deported back in December 2023 , more than a decade after his extradition was first sought. One former soldier testified that Barrientos had the habit of brandishing his pistol and declaring: “I killed Víctor Jara with this!” Barrientos was eventually arrested in the US after a routine traffic stop, and lost his US citizenship not because of his crimes, but on the grounds that he had failed to disclose his military background in his application. Jara’s widow died at the age of 96, just weeks before Barrientos was returned to Chile to face justice. Haase Mazzei’s defence has already requested his transfer from a prison in the southern city of Osorno to Punta Peuco, a well-appointed jail north of Santiago, built to house the human rights criminals of the Pinochet era. Core inflation rose by 0.1 percentage points, to 2.5%, marginally above the 2.4% expected by economists. August inflation is likely to be significantly higher, because of higher oil prices when the Donald Trump decided to renew bombing against Iran. Bert Colijn, chief economist for the Netherlands at ING, an investment bank, said: While energy inflation is on the move again, the question remains when second round effects will show up in core inflation data. The increase from 2.4% to 2.5% in core inflation in July was small, but does reflect both goods and services inflation trending slightly higher. We do expect goods inflation to still rise from the current inflation rate of 0.9% (an increase from 0.8% in June), but so far there has not been much movement. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/j.text: 0:43 Police footage shows scale of damage inside Aeon mall after explosion cause by Japan quake – video Japan Death toll in Japan earthquake rises to 30 as aftershock and heat hamper rescue efforts Soldiers and emergency teams search damaged shopping centre, paper mill and homes for survivors Earthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in pictures Gavin Blair in Tokyo Thu 30 Jul 2026 02.49 EDT First published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 22.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The death toll from the powerful earthquake that hit Japan on Tuesday has risen to 30, as the search for survivors trapped in a badly damaged shopping centre, paper mill and collapsed homes across the south-west of the country continues. ‘The shaking was terrifying’: stories of survival and loss emerge after Japan earthquake Read more The 6.8-magnitude quake, which struck Kumamoto prefecture on the island of Kyushu, injured at least 62 people, according to the prefectural government. Almost 5,000 Self-Defence Forces (SDF) personnel deployed to the region faced temperatures of up to 35C on Thursday, officials said, adding that a 5.8-magnitude aftershock overnight had further hampered the rescue efforts. Map of earthquake site About 170 rescue workers were searching the Aeon shopping centre in the town of Kashima, which was bustling with thousands of people when the quake struck. The company said about 3,000 customers were evacuated to a car park before a gas explosion occurred in another part of the shopping centre. Six of the 12 people pulled from the rubble have died. All those caught in the explosion were shop workers who had returned to the building after the evacuation, Aeon said. The company’s president bowed in apology at a press conference on Wednesday, saying Aeon had failed to anticipate the explosion, the cause of which was being investigated. 1:09 Aerial footage shows collapsed buildings after 6.8 magnitude Japan earthquake – video Japanese media footage from inside the shopping centre showed part of the ceiling had collapsed, with metal fragments and other debris scattered across the floor as helmeted, masked rescue workers searched the area. Police and SDF personnel were continuing to search for one worker in the debris at the Nippon Paper mill in Yatsushiro, where a chimney collapsed. Of the 10 others who were trapped, eight died and two were injured. In the first reported death of a foreign national, a Vietnamese technical intern was killed after a crane fell on him at the factory where he worked, according to the Vietnamese government. View image in fullscreen Nippon Paper mill, where a chimney collapsed. Photograph: Jiji Press/EPA Nearly 23,000 homes had no electricity and 75,000 had no running water, Kumamoto officials said. About 15,000 people had been evacuated to 400 shelters. The defence minister said on Wednesday evening that the SDF was airlifting coolers to shelters in Kumamoto, while SDF vessels were delivering water and food. “We’re doing everything possible to make saving lives a priority, making efforts to deliver life-saving supplies, beginning with water,” Shinjiro Koizumi said. Aerial police footage showed several homes had been flattened, including some that had crumbled into a river. View image in fullscreen A collapsed house in Hikawa, Kumamoto. Photograph: Kyodo/Reuters The earthquake registered the maximum level 7 on Japan’s seven-level shindo scale. “It was the strongest quake I have ever experienced,” Kanzo Matsumoto, 73, the operator of a luxury hot spring inn in Yatsushiro, told Agence France-Presse. The national Geospatial Information Authority said parts of the ground had shifted by 87cm during the quake. Yatsushiro town hall sustained damage to its base-isolation system, an earthquake-resistant technology designed to protect buildings by cushioning their foundations against intense shaking. The system was rebuilt after a deadly earthquake in 2016. View image in fullscreen Vehicles are crushed under collapsed buildings in Yatsushiro, south-western Japan. Photograph: Hiro Komae/AP Some car and semiconductor manufacturers with plants in Kyushu have halted production. Toyota said it would pause operations at three plants while it assessed the quake’s impact on suppliers and ⁠logistics. Honda suspended operations at a motorcycle plant until Friday. Taiwan’s TSMC has resumed operations at its Kumamoto facility, while Sony, Renesas Electronics and Tokyo Electron have halted production. Kyushu is ‌an important hub for Japan’s automotive and semiconductor industries, which account for about 20% of the region’s industrial output. Analysts said the shutdowns appeared to be driven largely by precaution than damage to production facilities. Kumamoto was struck by two devastating earthquakes in 2016 that killed 273 people and injured more than 2,800.The archipelago, home to about 125 million people, usually experiences hundreds of jolts every year and accounts for about 18% of the world’s earthquakes. https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text: Emergency workers are continuing their search for survivors in southern Japan after yesterday’s powerful earthquake left widespread devastation, with buildings collapsed, roads severely damaged and emergency teams digging through rubble. At least 13 people have been killed and many reported missing after the earthquake struck the Kumamoto area on the southern main island of Kyushu with a magnitude of 7.1, according to the Japan meteorological agency. The US Geological Survey measured it at magnitude 6.8. The Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said rescue workers faced a “race against time” to reach more people still trapped in rubble. “We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can,” she said. Eight people ⁠were pulled from the rubble of a partially collapsed Aeon shopping centre near the city of Kumamoto following an apparent explosion that occurred around an hour after the earthquake, according to reports. Photograph: Naoki Hiraoka/Kyodo News/AP View image in fullscreen Rescuers work at a collapsed house in Hikawa on Wednesday, a day after the earthquake. Photograph: Naoki Hiraoka/Kyodo News/AP Japan ‘The shaking was terrifying’: stories of survival and loss emerge after Japan earthquake Rescuers pulling people from the wreckage in southern Japan in a haunting repeat of disaster that struck 10 years ago ‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing Gavin Blair in Tokyo Wed 29 Jul 2026 05.08 EDT Last modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “T here was a voice coming from the collapsed house, and I could see a hand,” Tomohide Nagata, a volunteer firefighter, told the Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbun. “One of our senior members crawled in and pulled him out. He was bleeding from the head, but I’m so glad he survived.” Nagata had heard a noise coming from one completely flattened home in the rural town of Hikawa, close to the epicentre of Tuesday’s 6.8-magnitude earthquake in southern Japan. The town was one of the areas hardest hit, with numerous older houses collapsing. Terrified of the ongoing aftershocks, many residents spent Tuesday night in their cars outside Hikawa’s town hall, where staff distributed food and drinks. ‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing Read more At least 13 people were killed and hundreds injured when the earthquake struck the island of Kyushu. The prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said on Wednesday: “There are people who are still waiting to be rescued, and it’s a race against time. We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can.” Iwaoka Shigemi, 79, and his wife, Michiyo, 77, had escaped from their house and spent the night sleeping in their car in Hikawa, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. With temperatures expected to reach 35C on Wednesday, they were now worried about the risk of heatstroke. Suemi Nagata, 79, was unable to escape Hikawa by car because her garage had been destroyed but had made it to the town hall with her husband and older sister. “The lateral shaking was worse than the Kumamoto earthquake 10 years ago, and it was terrifying,” she told the town’s local newspaper. “Just to have survived with my life is something to be grateful for.” View image in fullscreen A damaged road in Hikawa. Photograph: Kyodo/Reuters In April, the prefecture of Kumamoto commemorated the 10th anniversary of the 2016 earthquake that killed more than 275 people and caused widespread devastation. In that case, a 6.2-magnitude foreshock was followed two days later by the deadly 7-magnitude quake, something that will be on the mind of tens of thousands across Kumamoto in the week ahead. At the Kumamoto Aeon mall, which was severely damaged by what is understood to have been a gas explosion triggered by the earthquake, a number of employees had gone back inside after evacuating customers and were caught in the blast. A 16-year-old girl who got out with other shoppers moments before the explosion, told the Asahi Shimbun she “felt completely safe once she was outside”, only to be left struggling to breathe by dust and smoke. A 74-year-old man who often shopped at the mall told the Nikkei newspaper that he had just learned that an acquaintance who worked there was hurt. “I could have been caught up in it myself,” he said. Up to 30 employees were initially reported trapped inside and four remain missing. View image in fullscreen A rescue worker walks in front of the Aeon mall, which was damaged by an explosion after the earthquake. Photograph: Hiro Komae/AP In nearby Uki City, which also experienced shaking ranked at the maximum 7 on the Japanese shindo scale, residents told of lucky escapes and heartbreaking unsuccessful rescue efforts. Earthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in pictures Read more A woman in her 40s had managed to get to an evacuation shelter with three generations of her family after putting herself between falling furniture and her children. “I was pinned under a chest of drawers at home. I protected my children and then hurried to evacuate,” she told the Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbun from Toyono elementary school, which was being used as an evacuation shelter after the ceiling of the local disaster facility fell in. On Tuesday evening as neighbours and relatives attempted to check in on each other, residents in the Asakawa district of Uki found one house flattened, with roof tiles scattered on the ground around where it had once stood. As family members looked on, a handful of volunteer firefighters attempted to rescue an elderly man trapped inside. “The man is a childhood friend of mine,” the visibly shaken 70-year-old head of the local district told the Kumamoto newspaper. “We tried to pull him out, but the aftershocks came one after another, so we had no choice but to give up.” As in Hikawa, many Uki residents slept in their cars, and local government workers handed out water and food. Unable to use the damaged disaster facility, the city set up a makeshift response headquarters in a car park. In Yatsushiro, south of Hikawa, one man’s life may have been saved by his schedule when his workplace, a single-storey wooden structure, collapsed. “It was a day off and I wasn’t at work, so I escaped with my life,” said the self-employed man, 63, who spent the night in a tent pitched in his garden. “Though I have no idea what I’ll do starting tomorrow.” Explore more on these topics Japan Earthquakes Asia Pacific features Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Death toll in Japan earthquake rises to 30 as aftershock and heat hamper rescue efforts 'People are waiting to be rescued': race under way to find Japan quake survivors – video ‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing Earthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in pictures Dashcam captures moment 6.8-magnitude earthquake hits Japan – video Japan earthquake injures at least 100 and kills two inside shopping mall Aerial footage shows collapsed buildings after 6.8 magnitude Japan earthquake – video Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: More than 80 dead and dying greater crested terns have been spotted off the South Australian coast in what is a suspected H5N1 bird flu mass mortality event. Photograph: imageBROKER/David & Micha Sheldon/Getty Images/imageBROKER RF View image in fullscreen More than 80 dead and dying greater crested terns have been spotted off the South Australian coast in what is a suspected H5N1 bird flu mass mortality event. Photograph: imageBROKER/David & Micha Sheldon/Getty Images/imageBROKER RF Bird flu First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds Helicopter surveillance finds dead and dying greater crested terns off South Australian coast as H5 virus spreads Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Graham Readfearn Environment and climate correspondent Sat 1 Aug 2026 02.12 EDT Last modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 04.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 80 dead and sick birds seen on rocks off the South Australian coast are suspected to be the first mass mortality event from the deadly H5N1 bird flu virus, only six weeks after the disease arrived in Australia. Authorities reported on Saturday that helicopter surveillance had revealed 49 dead greater crested terns on Baudin Rocks, near Robe, as well as 35 more sick terns. While some of the birds had been collected for testing, South Australia’s chief vet Skye Freuan said it was likely the first mass mortality event from the disease. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email South Australia also reported three suspected positive cases in other greater crested terns, including one inland at Monarto, suggesting the disease has begun moving away from the coast. The Monarto area is home to several poultry farms. Three silver gulls were also suspected positive, SA authorities said, adding to the first silver gull found a few days ago and confirmed positive by the CSIRO earlier on Saturday. Kate Millar, the chief executive of conservation charity BirdLife Australia, called it a “very significant escalation of the bird flu situation in Australia, and a very bleak milestone”. “Sadly, we’re at the beginning of a long and challenging battle and birds and wildlife are going to need all the help they can get,” she said. Jack Gough, the chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said it now appeared the disease was “starting to take off” and “mirroring the experience in South America of early detections, then rapid increases in numbers and spread leading to mass mortality events in wildlife.” “We are still at the very early stages of this devastating disease spreading, but the possible first mass mortality coming just days after the virus was declared not eradicable indicates how quickly this could escalate,” he said. Freuan said there was “nothing we can do” to stop the spread of the disease, but that surveillance was working. The news came at the end of a significant week in the development of the disease when numbers jumped by 20 in just a few days to the current total of 53. Australia was the last continent to have the unwelcome arrival of a disease that has killed millions of birds and mammals around the world. Victoria this week confirmed its first cases of the virulent strain in a greater crested tern found in Portland, with the state joining Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales and Queensland that have all recorded positive cases. On Saturday, Victorian authorities said samples from five crested terns had been sent to the CSIRO laboratory in Geelong, with preliminary testing suggesting more positive results. Five confirmed cases in birds at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island also raised concerns for the welfare of the area’s Australian sea lions – an endangered species. Tens of thousands of seals have died worldwide from the disease. But it has been the cases among silver gulls that has experts like Sean Dooley, the national affairs adviser at BirdLife Australia, concerned that the spread of the virus has now reached a critical new stage. “When people think of a seagull, they’re almost always thinking of the silver gull,” said Dooley. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Australian sea lions, an endangered species, are at risk of contracting H5N1 bird flu. Photograph: Brad Leue/Alamy “They’re very common, and primarily they are coastal, but they do come inland and can turn up in Lake Eyre following floods,” said Dooley. Silver gulls are the second Australian native species to catch the disease, after dozens of detections in greater crested terns. But it is the silver gull’s behaviour and habits that have experts concerned because they scavenge from dead or dying animals, meaning they can easily pick up the disease from other sick birds. They also pick detritus from water bodies – lakes and flooded areas included – and these are known to be breeding grounds for the disease. “There is such a large population of silver gulls, and they move into other habitats. They could be the vector that takes bird flu inland,” says Dooley. “They’re also really successful in urban areas and could bring the disease into those bird populations.” Because Australia has a high concentration of unique birds, the susceptibility of many native species isn’t known. But the fears are there is no reason to think they would manage any better than birds overseas. Birds that flock around water have tended to be the hardest hit. Examples include sandwich terns, black-headed gulls and northern gannets in Europe and, in Peru, pelicans. Dooley said the mood at BirdLife Australia this week had been one of “trying to suppress that sinking, gut-churning feeling”. The winter season for birdwatchers along the coast had been one of the best in 10 years, said Dooley, with rare petrels turning up in numbers along the east coast. “Now that has been heavily tinged because probably among those were birds carrying H5N1.” Explore more on these topics Bird flu Wildlife Birds Marine life Animals news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text: Adani will pay no tax this financial year despite generating about $1bn in revenue from coal mining in Queensland. Photograph: Wikimedia View image in fullscreen Adani will pay no tax this financial year despite generating about $1bn in revenue from coal mining in Queensland. Photograph: Wikimedia Adani Group Adani to pay no company tax despite $1bn revenue from Queensland coalmine Indian conglomerate offsets earnings from Carmichael mine to report $340.6m loss, after promising billions in taxes and royalties Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Jonathan Barrett Business editor Fri 31 Jul 2026 20.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 22.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Indian conglomerate Adani will pay no company tax despite generating almost $1bn in revenue from coal mining in Queensland over the past year. Financial accounts show the Carmichael thermal coal operations used large costs – including production and related party logistics expenses – to offset its $963.5m revenue in the 12 months to 31 March. This resulted in a recorded $340.6m loss for the year, erasing its tax bill. Guardian Australia analysis of company accounts shows the mining project has never paid corporate tax after opening in 2021, despite past pledges by Adani that the operations would plough billions of dollars in taxes and royalties into the economy. Adani donated $600,000 to Liberal National party before 2024 state election using federal ‘loophole’ Read more Adani Mining’s accounts show that it paid $58m in royalties in the 12-month period. Royalties are payments made to governments to extract state-owned minerals. Adani also paid a $33.1m royalty to a related party. Tim Buckley, a former investment banker and the director of Climate Energy Finance, said the company was structured so that it wouldn’t pay corporate tax in Australia. “This is a perfect example of why Australia needs new rules that ensure foreign entities have a sensible capital structure,” said Buckley, who advocates for changes that would limit the amount of deductions a business can make to reduce tax. Adani’s project approval in central Queensland’s Galilee Basin was fiercely contested , opening a new jurisdiction of thermal coal extraction that raised environmental concerns. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Industry groups supporting the conglomerate had claimed Adani’s project would fund schools, hospitals and other infrastructure for “almost a century” through mining taxes and royalties. A spokesperson for Adani Mining said the project provided direct jobs for more than 1,400 Queenslanders last financial year. “We comply fully with our state and commonwealth taxation and royalty obligations and our statutory profit and tax outcomes are determined in accordance with Australian accounting standards and the corporations act,” the spokesperson said. The Carmichael operations opened during a prosperous time for coalminers. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sent global energy prices soaring in 2022. Coal prices are now also being supported by energy supply constraints caused by conflict in the Middle East. The Adani-controlled Abbot Point port business, named North Queensland Export Terminal, also did not pay any company tax over the most recent 12-month reporting period, despite earning $356.6m. Various operating expenses lead to a $6.8m loss, with no tax payable. The terminal business’s chief executive, Mark Smith, said accounts were prepared in accordance with Australian accounting standards and reflect the capital-intensive nature of owning and operating major export infrastructure. “The terminal plays an important role in supporting Queensland trade and we remain focused on delivering safe, reliable, and efficient export services for our customers,” Smith said. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: William Standish lost contact with his family as he was hiking in Wyoming. Photograph: Teton county search and rescue View image in fullscreen William Standish lost contact with his family as he was hiking in Wyoming. Photograph: Teton county search and rescue Wyoming Missing Australian hiker found dead in Wyoming, officials say Body of William Standish discovered in Teton mountains as investigators say fatal fall likely cause of death Edward Helmore Fri 31 Jul 2026 17.06 EDT Last modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 17.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 28-year-old Australian hiker who lost contact with his family while hiking the Continental Divide Trail between Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks in Wyoming has been found dead, according to authorities. The man, identified as William Standish, was discovered by rescuers on Wednesday morning in the Wigwams, a series of rocky peaks on the west slope of the Teton mountain range, the Teton county coroner said. Investigators say it was likely he suffered a fatal fall. Standish had been attempting a thru-hike of the Continental Divide Trail between the Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks when he disappeared after contacting his family on 23 July, according to a statement from Teton county rescuers. Evidence suggests Standish may have fallen from a steep ridgeline that separates Grand Teton and the Jedediah Smith wilderness, officials said. Standish was discovered by a helicopter team after it spotted an orange backpack – and then saw his remains below the ridge. His family said it had stopped receiving updates from him via a Garmin GPS device and Facebook Messenger on 23 July, leading to a search being mounted by Teton county rescue crews. On 19 July, Standish gave an update from a location near Old Faithful, and described his planned route in the Tetons, Gros Ventre wilderness, the Wind River range, and the Divide Basin. Four days later, the family received a Garmin check-in without coordinates or a message. There was also a Facebook Messenger video that they believe placed him in the Wigwams. The Teton county search and rescue team said it “sends its sincere condolences to the family and friends of the deceased”. It also expressed gratitude to federal agencies who assisted in searching for Standish. Standish had reportedly been following a popular thru-hike, or end-to-end through-hike, starting in Canada, the most northern point of the 3,100-mile Continental Divide Trail – which passes down through Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, and New Mexico. There have been other hiking-related deaths in North America recently. The Colorado Sun reported that a 15-year-old boy died after being struck by lightning on the state’s Mount Blue Sky on Monday. Sheriff’s officials identified the boy as Levi Strobel. Four other people were seriously injured, including Levi’s younger brother. In Arizona, a man died during a hike on Phoenix’s South Mountain. Richard Fletcher, 61, left his home early on Saturday morning. Investigators later said his death was consistent with a heat-related or medical event, authorities told local media . A 62-year-old man died in New Hampshire when he suffered a medical emergency in the state’s Welch-Dickey trail in the White Mountains. He was evacuated by national guard helicopter and later pronounced dead, according to New Hampshire Public Radio . Two hikers also died in Canada’s Banff national park. One was a woman in her 20s after falling from a mountain near Marvel Peak on Tuesday. Three days earlier, a 65-year-old from Calgary fell from Mount Temple, also in Banff, the CBC reported. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: File photo: The NSW Ombudsman has identified ‘inadequate policies and procedures’ regarding how Homes NSW deals with tenants’ complaints. Photograph: Dean Sewell/AAP View image in fullscreen File photo: The NSW Ombudsman has identified ‘inadequate policies and procedures’ regarding how Homes NSW deals with tenants’ complaints. Photograph: Dean Sewell/AAP New South Wales NSW should compensate elderly woman whose public housing was inundated with sewage, ombudsman finds Ombudsman finds Homes NSW acted unreasonably and recommended additional payment for distress and suffering Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Achol Arok Fri 31 Jul 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 22.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An elderly public housing tenant whose home was damaged by sewage overflows will be fully compensated by the New South Wales government after it disposed of her personal belongings without her consent and failed to properly support her insurance claim. The NSW Ombudsman on Friday published its report after an investigation in which it found Homes NSW acted unreasonably in how it handled the tenant’s contaminated belongings and “failed to provide full and accurate information to the insurer”. The woman, whose name and suburb were not made public, had lived in the unit for more than 15 years. She reported three successive sewage overflows within three months, which saw raw sewage enter the property. After the third incident she was relocated, but her belongings remained in the contaminated unit for two months before being boxed up and moved to a vacant property. ‘I would just like to see more people housed’: inside NSW’s social housing changes Read more The furniture, household items, and family heirlooms were not cleaned nor returned to her, despite Homes NSW telling her “she would be actively involved in the decision to keep or dispose of any items”. She was later told “she would be adequately compensated” through an insurance claim, according to the report. When the claim was lodged, the insurer denied liability and offered a small “goodwill” payment. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The report found Homes NSW’s failure to provide the insurer with “full and accurate information” which contributed to the rejection of the claim. The ombudsman’s recommendations included an apology and full compensation “in accordance with her itemised compensation claim”. It also recommended an additional payment for “the distress and suffering she experienced while trying to resolve her claim over more than five years”. Homes NSW has accepted all of the recommendations and will implement them by next month, according to the report. The senior deputy ombudsman for complaints and investigations, Kate Anderson, said the findings and recommendations come after identifying “inadequate policies and procedures in place”. “There were several points where there was inadequate communication to her about … what next steps were going to follow and then those steps were ultimately not followed,” she said. Anderson said the case demonstrated the importance of ensuring agencies were able to “listen to their complainants”, particularly when they should “have engaged with this particular individual to reach a conclusion on this complaint far earlier”. “This individual actually had very good record of the possessions that she had and the respective value of them, which ultimately was not taken into consideration,” she said. “At all points, people should be treated with courtesy and respect and the situation that materialised here really demonstrated that ultimately by the time it had come to us, the tenant had been trying to resolve it herself with Home NSW for a number of years and hadn’t been able to get an effective resolution.” A spokesperson for Homes NSW said it “sincerely apologises to the tenant affected” and acknowledged “the distress, inconvenience and impact the situation has had on them”. Homes NSW has since introduced “a number of changes to how we deliver maintenance and repairs with the aim of improved tenant satisfaction, including establishing an in-house call centre to manage repair requests”, the spokesperson said.
